episodes.170551: An organized west-to-east line of early morning thunderstorms tracked from east-central Illinois into central Indiana.  Strong upper level winds and ample vertical wind shear combined with adequate instability to produce severe winds generally parallel to, and north of Interstate 70.  Strongest winds were found where the wind shear was best oriented to the squall line's progression:  across the Indianapolis metro area and points east.  A gustnado in Anderson (Madison County) also caused minor damage.  The episode's strongest winds likely occurred in the evening when a more isolated thunderstorm impacted Rush County.
episodes.170557: Monsoon season got off to an early start, and that momentum continued throughout the entire month of July with yet another very busy and active day on July 31, 2022. Per usual, thunderstorms developed early in the day across the high terrain areas before becoming more widespread throughout the evening. Many of these thunderstorms were capable of producing heavy rain which resulted in flash flooding reports across the area. The Calf Canyon burn scar was hit again with flash flooding and debris flow near Gascon while flash flooding across western New Mexico forced the closure of a few roadways.
episodes.170560: Despite the high pressure centered more over western New Mexico, an abundant amount of moisture still resided within the atmosphere. This led to scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across much of the central and western New Mexico, some of which produced very heavy rainfall. Flash flooding and even a report of large hail was reported across portions of central New Mexico.
episodes.170607: Mid level tropical moisture from Hurricane Frank which was situated off the Baja coast spread northward into southern and central California on August 1.  This moisture interacted with a very warm and unstable airmass which was present over the region at the time.  Showers and thunderstorms broke out during the afternoon and brought moderate to locally heavy rainfall to the mountains and deserts of eastern Kern County as well as to the Sierra Nevada.  The heavier thunderstorms prompted the issuance of two Flash Flood Warnings, two Flood Advisories and three Significant Weather Advisories.  There were reports of nuisance street flooding as a result of the heavy rainfall.
episodes.170626: An upper level disturbance passing along a stationary front draped across the lower Mid-Atlantic region triggered spotty thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening of July 31st.  Of particular note was the deep tropical moisture situated across the region, with precipitable water values across the Piedmont estimated to be around 2.2 inches per Storm Prediction Center Meso-Analysis, or about 2 standard deviations above normal for late July.  Though few, there were breaks in the cloud cover during the afternoon and early evening, which allowed for increased surface heating, with surface-based CAPE values rising to 2,000 J/Kg prior to the storm.  Windflow in the low levels of the atmosphere was nearly unidirectional from the west, which promoted a brief period of training with a second cell developing around 9:00 PM EDT just behind the initial cell to prolong the heavy rainfall across the southern end of Lynchburg.
episodes.170723: Abundant monsoon moisture remained over the Four Corners region. Additionally, a shortwave disturbance moved overhead. This led to widespread showers and thunderstorms across western Colorado. Storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain. Some storms produced localized debris flows across the region.
episodes.170898: A couple of thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts over the upper tidal Potomac River and upper Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.171134: A surge of monsoonal moisture coupled with a pre-storm environment of steepened late afternoon lapse rates and modest shear from an upper short wave lifting north-northeast over the region produced discrete thunderstorms capable of heavy downpours and large hail over Plumas and Lassen counties.
episodes.171293: Several days of monsoon thunderstorms impacted the mountains and High Desert in Southern California. The San Bernardino County Mountains were particularly hard hit. Torrential downpours led to flash flooding and debris flows, including over the El Dorado burn scar.
episodes.171430: A midlevel shortwave trough was situated over the Upper Midwest Sunday night (31st) into Monday morning (1st). At the surface, a strong occluded low was also present. From this low and occlusion, a warm front extended to the southeast, lifting through the Commonwealth during the same time frame. A MCS developed in the Upper Mississippi Valley and continued to push southeast towards the Commonwealth during the morning hours. This prompted SPC to put portions of northern and eastern KY in a slight risk for severe weather throughout the day. Ironically, we did not see any severe weather out of this system - however, showers that developed during the morning hours ahead of the MCS were a different story. These showers developed over the eastern portion of the state, and impacted areas that were already heavily saturated from the devastating rains that occurred the week before. More so, the convection was moving parallel to the mean flow, which meant that many of these showers continued to train over the same locations for an extended period of time. This prompted flash flood warnings, and led to impacts in Martin, Pike, Letcher, Floyd, and Knott counties.
episodes.171436: Small clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast across the lower Wabash Valley during the late afternoon and evening hours. Large hail was reported with a couple of these storms. The storms initially formed along the residual outflow boundary left by an early morning thunderstorm complex. The atmosphere was very unstable during the late afternoon and early evening, when peak mixed-layer capes approached 4000 J/kg. Once the storms formed an organized cold pool, new thunderstorms developed on the western flank of the storm complex as an unstable southwest wind flow was lifted over the cold pool.
episodes.171437: A cluster of severe thunderstorms with widespread damaging winds affected the Evansville area. The storms initially formed over Illinois and west central Indiana along the residual outflow boundary left by an early morning thunderstorm complex. The atmosphere was very unstable during the late afternoon and early evening, when peak mixed-layer capes approached 4000 J/kg. Once the storms formed an organized cold pool, new thunderstorms developed on the western flank of the storm complex as an unstable southwest wind flow was lifted over the cold pool.
episodes.171441: Monsoonal moisture allowed for another round of thunderstorms to develop over the San Bernardino Mountains on August 1st. Slow-moving storms allowed for efficient rainfall production, which led to flash flooding in the town of Big Bear and also over portions of Highway 38.
episodes.171454: Low pressure drew in a cold front beginning on the afternoon of August 1st. In advance of this feature, afternoon heating and residing unstable conditions contributed to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. Antecedent rainfall ahead of this event resulted in susceptible soil conditions, which coupled with heavy rainfall that day led to areas of flash flooding.||Mingo County was inundated with heavy rain on the morning of the 1st and continued to see rain occur into the early afternoon. The quick rise and continued deluge of water of the local creeks and streams resulted in flooding along the adjacent roadways. Residential bridges were washed out as a result of these heavy rains and also damage to several homes within the county.||The cold front arrived into West Virginia on the morning of August 2nd, which continued the threat for flash flooding across the eastern portions of the state. The boundary stalled nearby that afternoon, leading to several rounds of showers and strong thunderstorms. Braxton County observed a combination of strong winds and heavy rainfall, resulting in downed trees and flooded roadways.
episodes.171477: A stalled frontal boundary and surface low pressure south of the state early Sunday morning began to slowly lift northward into the southeast and south-central portion of the state throughout the day. Showers and thunderstorms developed along the boundary and moved eastward. Since the system as whole showed very little forward progression, multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms ended up moving across the same locations multiple times, on top of already saturated soils. This ended up leading to multiple instances of flash flooding, specifically in Whitley and Pike Counties.
episodes.171730: A supercell embedded in a large thunderstorm cluster produced severe wind gusts in a part of far southwest Nebraska.
episodes.172017: Low pressure moved across central Minnesota the afternoon and evening of July 31, with a trailing cold front moving across southern Minnesota.  Several storms developed, including one low topped mini supercell that produced a brief tornado.
episodes.172071: Remnants of a mesoscale convective system created a few supercells in eastern Ohio that advanced into northern West Virginia/western Pennsylvania. Two tornadoes spun up from a single supercell. Despite meager instability, deep-layer wind shear was favorable at near 40 knots, and the storm tracked in a favorable direction to ingest rotating updrafts.
episodes.172141: Weak southwest steering flow and high moisture resulted in locally heavy rainfall across NE FL where the sea breezes and boundaries merge in the afternoon and evening.
episodes.172248: An isolated severe thunderstorm caused some damage.
episodes.172375: Remnants of a mesoscale convective system created a few supercells in eastern Ohio that advanced into northern West Virginia/western Pennsylvania. Two tornadoes spun up from a single supercell. Despite meager instability, deep-layer wind shear was favorable at near 40 knots, and the storm tracked in a favorable direction to ingest rotating updrafts.
episodes.172417: Isolated severe storms with gusty winds developed along a nearly stationary warm front near the Virginia/North Carolina border on July 31.
episodes.172555: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the northeast to east-central Texas Panhandle on the evening of the 31st. Given the good instability across the region, these storms were strong enough to create severe wind gusts.
episodes.172690: Scattered thunderstorms moved northwest across southeast Arizona during the afternoon and evening. Heavy rain over the Bighorn Fire burn scar resulted in flash flooding in Finger Rock Canyon. Several homes and an assisted living facility were flooded in the Catalina Foothills. Flash flooding also occurred in Nogales and in western Pima County. Large hail and isolated wind damage were observed in parts of the Tucson Metro area.
episodes.172802: A weak warm frontal passage aided convective downpours in a weak steering environment.
episodes.172913: The stormy period which began on the 24th continued to bring severe weather and flash flooding through the end of the month.
episodes.172914: The stormy period which began on the 24th continued to bring severe weather and flash flooding through the end of the month.
episodes.172996: A cold front extending from Wisconsin into eastern Iowa triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms during the pre-dawn hours of August 1st.  The storms tracked southeastward, producing scattered wind damage along and north of the I-72 corridor.  One of the cells spawned a brief EF-1 tornado in the town of Beason in eastern Logan County which severely damaged a grain elevator and numerous trees before quickly lifting.  Another storm produced a brief EF-0 tornado near Mason City in Mason County that caused minor damage.
episodes.172999: An outflow boundary from convection earlier in the day served as the primary focusing mechanism for numerous storm clusters along and south of I-70 from the late afternoon  of August 1st into the pre-dawn hours of August 2nd.  Some of the storms dropped very large hail up to 2 inches in diameter.  In addition, continuous back-building cells produced a swath of heavy rainfall in excess of 8 inches from eastern Effingham County across Jasper County into northeastern Richland County.  As a result, many roads were closed due to flash flooding.  The flooding lingered until around midday on August 2nd, particularly in the hardest hit locations from Dietrich in Effingham County to Newton in Jasper County.
episodes.173047: Thunderstorms moving through Tuscola County brought down trees and spawned two weak tornadoes.
episodes.173081: As a weak upper level trough passed through the region, moisture from the Gulf of Mexico began to move inland across the region. Daytime heating combined with increased lift from the upper level trough moving through promoted thunderstorm development. One storm was able to intensify to a severe level and produce damaging winds.
episodes.173105: Thunderstorms developed across the state on August 1, with several producing damaging outflow winds across northern Utah and isolated flash flooding in central Utah.
episodes.173163: The combination of abundant low-level moisture along with MLCAPE of greater than 1000 J/KG led to the development of terrain-induced thunderstorm activity across portions of Joshua Tree National Park during the early to mid-afternoon hours.
episodes.173214: Scattered thunderstorms developed late in the afternoon through early evening. A couple storms became severe, producing damaging winds.
episodes.173252: Residual monsoon moisture and mostly sunny conditions in the morning allowed for a few thunderstorms to form over northern Arizona.
episodes.173307: River flooding from snowmelt and rainfall earlier this spring continued into August, though rivers would see a slow decline due to drier conditions. The James River at Ashton fell below flood stage on August 15th at 18:15 CST, while the gauges at Stratford and Columbia remained in flood stage the entire month.
episodes.173389: Scattered severe thunderstorms in advance of a weak frontal boundary produced damaging winds across portions of southeast Virginia.
episodes.173390: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a weak frontal boundary produced gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.173391: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a weak frontal boundary produced gusty winds across portions of the James River.
episodes.173392: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a weak frontal boundary produced gusty winds across portions of the northeast North Carolina Coastal Waters.
episodes.173456: A surface low moving across Minnesota and Wisconsin drug a cold front across northwest Illinois during the early morning hours of August 1st. Showers and thunderstorms developed across the area ahead of the front.  There was sufficient shear and instability for these storms to produce sporadic hail up to an inch and an isolated damaging wind gust.
episodes.173542: A sea-breeze induced outflow boundary pushed northward in the afternoon on August 1st. A cluster of storms developed along the outflow boundary, and produced isolated wind damage in Montgomery County.
episodes.173548: Dry weather resulted in a gradual drop in water levels along the James River through the month, and flooding ended during early- to mid-month.
episodes.173789: Broad east to southeast flow advected in monsoon moisture, which fueled thunderstorms over southeast California. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173790: Broad east to southeast flow advected in monsoon moisture, which fueled thunderstorms over southern Nevada. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173931: A weak warm frontal passage aided convective downpours in a weak steering environment as it moved northward.

Other roads that observed flooding within the township included Dickenson Street, 4th Avenue, Route 49, and Highway 52. Widespread damaging winds from 60 to 70 mph swept across the Evansville metropolitan area from north to south. A few businesses suffered roof  damage. Hundreds of trees were snapped, uprooted, or had large branches broken. Some of the trees landed across power lines. Some downed trees blocked roads. Numerous power outages occurred. Up to 28,000 electric customers in and near Evansville were without power in the aftermath of the storm. The first report of a downed tree and power lines was about ten miles north of downtown Evansville, or three miles northeast of Darmstadt. Tree damage became more widespread as the storms moved across the north side of the Evansville metro area and then across downtown Evansville. A peak wind gust of 68 mph was measured by the Evansville airport automated observing system. The duration of wind gusts above 60 mph lasted for at least four minutes at the airport. There was an unofficial measured gust of 62 mph a couple miles south of Darmstadt.
A few three-foot diameter trees were snapped and blown over.
